projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Jeanne O'Hare was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: It is October 05, 2005. We are at Mrs. O'Hare's house. Mrs. Jean O'Hare is the only interviewee. Megan Engle is camera operator. When is your birthday?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: I was eighty-three years old August 27. I was born in 1922.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What kind of work did you perform?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: During World War II, I was with the army ordinance. First I inspected machine gun, which was when it was fidget air. Then I was sent to Delco, and I inspected the shells that the tanks used finally I went to NCR, and I inspected shells again. We had to use a cremator and we also had to attach some kind of acid the government had purchased in the shape of a flaming bomb and army ordinance signature and we would stamp the part we had inspected and that would show it was alright to use.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What is your name? Your maiden name?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: My maiden was Anderson.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Where were you born and raised?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: I was born in Green County in a little town called Fairfield but now is known as Fairborn.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What is your family's background? Mostly educational?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: My dad went through his sophomore year in high school and he was raised on a farm. He lived in Pennsylvania. My mom lived in licking county, Ohio near Columbus. My mother's parents were very poor and took my mother out of school in the sixth grade to work on different farms as an assistant.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What is your current address?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: 5276 cobbler gate drive apt. I. I live in moraine.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: At the time of the war were you in a relationship or married?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: I was single.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What was your spouse's name and wartime occupation or did you have a spouse?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: I didn't marry until after the war.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Where did you work or live in the war?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: When I first started I still lived at home, then I moved to old north Dayton, in a cottage that had three bedrooms and the landlord rented each of the rooms to two girls, so there was six girls.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What was your main wartime activity?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Of course you worked seven days a week and you were not encouraged to take vacations because ordinance was needed for the boys that were fighting in the war. We girls that lived in the cottage often went to common's bowling alley and bowl and then there was a place in old north Dayton they had a live band on the weekend. We would always go there to dance and that's when girls danced with girls.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Where you employed outside the home?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: When the war first started I was working for Reynolds and Reynolds but I was doing war work. We were settling books for pilots who could train and I had taking a test and applied for the job in the ordinance inspector and shortly after the war soon as the factory could get from frigid air to machine guns they called me to work.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Were you in industry?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: I don't understand.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Were you authorized? Were you authorized?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: How did you feel about the unions?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: I am a union person.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: How did you feel about?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: I am sorry that it became a part of the criminal I'm sorry that It happened but in union itself, I think it was a good thing.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Did you devolve friendships during trains or the activity itself?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Yes in fact the picture that I gave to you if you turn it over on the back their names are on the back.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Did you have any family or friends in the service or doing war work?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: My dad worked at inland and my brother Paul quit school when he was sixteen and went to war. During war they could hire you and when and when you reach the day, I had a cousin who came up from LAN Chester, Ohio and stay with us and she was also In war work, and it was all war work. I don't know what they made at inland I never worked there.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: How did you feel about the war?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Oh everybody once we were attacked, which was a sneak attack we were all ready to fight and I was willing to do whatever I could do to help win the war and pf course everybody else felt the same way, because we had been attacked a sneak attack everybody was ready to fight back.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What was your family and friends feeling?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Well of course my brothers were to young to fight in the war but my brother Paul as soon as he turned seventeen he joined the navy but the war was over by the time he reached his seventeenth birthday.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Did you live with family friends or co-works?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: I did when the war started I lived at home then I left in 1944.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: In what ways did the war change your activities and habits?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Well so much was rationed, like you could only have three pairs of shoes a year, and sugar was rationed, of course gasoline was rationed soap powder was rationed but I didn't practically care for that and going in to get a candy bar was impossible because sugar was rationed and they had as far as gasoline was concerned if you had a car it had one of three stamps on it a,b,c. A only 3.5 gallons a week , someone like a minister could have a or b because he had to visit his parishioners, and d went to doctors and you know somebody or anybody if you was in the war you got at least a or b ticket.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Were you or others in your community treated differently because of their gender?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: No it was practically all girls that worked during the war because they were calling the men to duty so there was never no discrimination that I was aware of.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What were some of the first changes in your life after the war started?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: After the war started I started going to church and eventually joined the church I was Catholic.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What responsibilities did you have to take on?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: You had to watch like getting soap powder but of course me and the six other girls traded at the mom and pop store, because Kroger and lisle market were the only two big stores but we traded at this little mom and pop store. And they would save it for us.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What specials activities were you involved in at work or after work with co-workers?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Mostly we bowled or skated down at the skate land or we went to the north Dayton angers and drunk on the weekends and dance because they had live music and like I said that when girls danced together because there were no boys.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Did any of your co-workers get married?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Not until after the war was over because their fiancée's were all over seas, but one by one the first little girl that got married her name was sally and I forgot her boyfriends name.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Do you know what the weddings like?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: No she, they were all from out of town. They all came to Dayton to work, and sally she lived in Kentucky and I forget what the other girls names was she lived north in diddlley so we were never able to go to there weddings.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Did you worry that are side might not win?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: It was pretty tough at first because of course Japan created the biggest proper and when the war first started Japan was winning but by 1943 and especially 1944 we began to we took back the Philippines and all the orgy mountains, and if you've ever been to Washington you have seen the statue of the boys raising the flag on mount Nava chi mountain.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Did you know anyone who was killed or wounded in the war?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: I know of a man who was wounded and he was severely he had cope with walking because he was shot in the spine and I went to their wedding back after I saw her death notice in the paper and I went to the funeral and he was there In the wheel chair so I don't know if he is alive or not.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: So tell me about corresponding via letters or otherwise with friends or family in the service.

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: They eventually had what they called via mail which was on a sheet of paper, and if you wrote on it, it was rushed out. I wrote to about three soldiers and I guess they were all in Europe and the one had married an English girl and he stayed over there and the other two came home because of course they were free. I had many ideas because they would have dances and stuff for the soldiers. We would go down and entertain the soldiers.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What affects did the war have on your physical and mental health or others you knew? Did it have any affect on you?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: No I don't think so I was just so relieved when it was over because so many boys were dying even though I didn't know them, that was hard to take so we were all of us we were more than delighted and of course me be day that was victory In Europe and we didn't celebrate much then we still had Japan but when Japan surrendered there was a huge celebration downtown. Everyone went downtown and it was raining and there had been a lot of confetti thrown and it through just like mud it was sticking to the bottoms of our shoes but we didn't care. It was so wonderful to have the war over.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Do you think medical care changed because of the war?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Oh absolutely that to me was the biggest thing that happened due to the war. Before the war you could drive by a house and there would be a corn tine on it, scarlet lived in the area, and after the war they declared polio as a rave point. I know so many people that were crippled by polio and now it was almost wiped out.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Did you have a worth while experience?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: I was just happy to do whatever I could to help the war. Its perhaps the only time I could recall everyone being of one spirit. When the war everybody they before the war started there were a lot of what they called " dubs", and once Japan attacked us we were all ready and willing to fight.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What was your most memorable experience?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Surprisingly it was when you inspected machine guns they also had a building were they tried them out and make sure they worked properly and I had to go down and watch. They put ear muffs on us because the machine guns were so loud. they could fire as many as six at a time and they fired them into bails of hay that I remembered the most because they were so loud and that is were I learned to hate guns. Who was the most memorable character that you knew of? I forgot most of their names now.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What was your most humorous experience?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: The only humor we had was going to the movies, a comedy because we were all dedicated to winning this war.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Have you visited any memorials or participated in any commemorations of the war?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Yes I went to Hawaii and visited poncho cemetery were so many boys were killed and December 7 are buried and there was a news man named Ernie Pyle and he was loved by all the unlisted men.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Was there a lack of opportunities and friends because of the war?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Yes, gasoline was rationed and if you had to go some place you had to walk, so your space was limited because of the war.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: How did your community respond to the war and civil defenses initiatives?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Everybody pitched in everybody.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Did you have a victory garden or other ways to get enough food?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: My parents did.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: How did you cope with wartime shortages?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Here I told you we were only allowed to have three pairs of shoes and a lot of women liked shoes well it turned out Mexico sent shoes to America called hirachis and they were not rationed because it was material Mexico sold. Every one of the ladies owned at least one pair of hirachis or at least two or three pairs. I will never forget this one girl who worked with us, if it was raining she would wear her rain hirachis and when she got to work she put on her dry hirachis and put the wet ones on the radiator to dry and if it was still raining when we got off of work she put back on the wet hirachis and that's the thing I still remember very well.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What did the shoes look like?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: They were leather and had little leather straps about that wide and they had a toe but they were not fastened in the back, I'm sorry I didn't save a pair, but everybody every women owned a pair of hirachis.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Can you talk about recycling of rubber, grease or other commodities?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Oh yea, you saved all your grease, you were likely to buy bacon and eat it on Fridays, you could put all the grease together, I know while I was still at home, I can remember my mama taking big things of grease to a fire station and they took it from there.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: To what extent was there hoarding or black marketing in your area?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: There was quiet a bit of it.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: How did you feel about war news from news reels or radios?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: For the first ten we were losing. It hurt, and as soon as we got our second win we began to take back all them islands Philippines, we were very happy, but we were more determined than ever to bring an end to the war. Some people were very critical of how the war ended, the atom bomb, but that's a million Americans rights in fact I have a picture of were Japan had sent us all war prisoners were to be beheaded if we invaded Japan because they thought we would and we would have saved one American life, I was for it but not everybody was. But if it took care of them I would be all for that but some people haven't a shocked. We were just talking about the newsreels, and how you felt, now we are going to move on to the next set of questions.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Why did you choose the activity you did?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Well I think my mom had some influence in me working for the government. She thought the government paid well and of course they had clerks, so your earned and leave and your sick leave, but you were not allowed to use them but it accumulated so I think she was the one who influenced me because they advertised it In the paper that they were going to give a test for army ordinance inspectors and I went down and took the test and I passed.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What kind of training were you given?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: How to use my cremators, I can no longer describe them. It's been so long since I saw them to be able to judge the thickness and thinness of a part. They furnished all the instruments that you used and of course when you left you had to leave the instruments there.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What was your title?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: I was an army ordinance inspector.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What kind of activities did you perform?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Yea like I said since everything was rationed about the only things you had to do were either go to a movie or skating. Now they did have a place in downtown Dayton called lance's merry-go-round. We would get together and go there every now and then but it was kind of expensive, so that was a treat.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: So you were a machine gun inspector?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: So what did you like and dislike about it?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: The thing that I disliked the most was when we had to go down to the firing range because i didn't like the noise. Otherwise I didn't mind doing what I did, cause before I went to the government I was working at Reynolds and Reynolds making books for the pilots, now that was boring. I was very happy when the government called me because there you walked and walked around the table.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: At work what special rules or conventions did you have to follow?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Of course we had to keep are hands washed and they asked us not to use lotion on are hands because they didn't want to transfer the parts, so they were really strict about washing your hands cleanly so you didn't leave anything on them.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: With who did you work with at work any close friends or family?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: The only person I remember who worked with me inspecting machine guns was a lady named Hazel Wisemer, and we got to be good friends but I don't think she's still alive now because she was older than me. We seemed to hit it off together.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What did your husband do in the war?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: He was in the army and he drove what they call retrievers which a big tractor which pulls a long trailer and the trailer holds two tanks, and it was his job to the tanks and drive them to the front. He liked the job he did , except when he got to the front he wasn't with his concept and would sometimes miss his paycheck. He was very happy with the salvation army. He said they would right up to the front and he said that when he was going to have to take a couple days to get back, they would pack him a lunch or a sandwich so when he got back he was very fond of the salvation army, because he thought they did more than anybody else to help. The little guys not the officers.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: So you guys got married after the war?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Yes in 1949. I met him in 1947 in the bowling alley were all the girls went and then he would also go down to the Anderson gun club and we got to talking and one night he asked if he could walk me home, and it all started from there.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: So you guys introduced yourselves?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Yes, well we were at the bowling alley , everybody knew everybody, and I got acquainted with him, I cant say who introduced us cause we just sort of mangled to together. So I liked him very well and I didn't know he felt about me, until one day he invited me to come home and meet his mother. Then I knew I had it from there. Of course his mother was lovely but then she had a stroke and passed ten weeks before we married so our marriage had a sad part because we had already contacted an ambulance and a wheel chair so she could come to the wedding and see us get married but a my husband always said she was relieved that he was finally settling down and that she was ready to go home and I don't know it was a shock just ten weeks before we married.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Where were you married at?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: St. Josephs church down on second street close to downtown and that used to be able the Irish parish and my husband's baptism certificates were and all those years you had to have your baptism certificates before you could get married in the church and of course I was Baptized there so but a we just had a very nice wedding. My husband in the woke of the wedding there is a picture of us walking out and his face was real sad and when I asked him what was wrong, he told me he was thinking about his mother and how much he had longed for her to see him get married and I told him I think she saw it any how and that made him feel a whole lot better.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: What time were you actually released from the war?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: After the war was over they notified us by letter that are appointments were reassigned and I could have went on out to the base but at the time I dint want to. So I worked at roomers, and Elder John sons, which is now called Elder Beermans, then I worked at the NCR factory. But when I got married they didn't hire married women so they laid me off.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Where did your husband work? Or when was he released?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Well he drove trucks, big semi trucks that was why he was allowed to drive the retrievers that pulled the big tanks because he had experience driving the big tractors. The last eight or nine years we were married he got tired and said " he wanted to come home at night", so he went to the city and of course he went to Cincinnati but he was home every night and it was so nice to have him home but he was killed in a trucking accident back in 1968 and it is something that I will never get over because the man who had struck him was legally blind. It was in the morning and he was on his way to work and of course he didn't see my husband. My husband lived thirty- three hours or thirty- six. But the doctor said that if he had survived he would have probably been brain dead so I guess it was just as well. The priest read him his last rights and I learned to except , and we got along very well together and his loss is something I will never get over completely.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Is there something else you would like to talk about during your times in the war?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: In Dayton they all had street cars yet and I think there was one route for the trolley bus. They were just trying it out to see how or otherwise you had to drive the street car, which went right down the middle of street, so when you wanted to get on like downtown they put lines you had to stand while you waited for the street car and it really wasn't safe cause some people, I know one time we were waiting and a car came by and it caught the lady's coat through the winder and tour it off of her and never stopped, they probably was going on but the war started and they couldn't put no more trolley buses on and of course they took up all the tracks and sold it for metal and now of course the trolley buses come up to the side walk and you don't have to get in the street anymore.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Is there anything else you would like to mention about the war, or your time serving in the war?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: It's been so long ago.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: How long did you serve in the war?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: Four years. The war began In 1941, and it was over August 1945. Mr. Roosevelt was president at the time and elected for the fourth term and he was elected in November and passed in April and Mr. Truman who was the vice president at the time took over and Mr. Truman was the president who made the ruling president who served two terms.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: Is there anything else you would like to add?

sp.speaker: Jeanne O'Hare
sp.p: I could probably think of more when you leave but I of course my daddy always had a garden and even after I left home, when I would I come home to visit he had tomatoes, and cucumbers.

sp.speaker: Megan Engle
sp.p: I guess that will be the end of the interview and this has been the interview and this had been the interview of jean O'Hare, October 05, 2005, it ended at 5:45 pm.
